div.p: This paper presents a flexible quantile spatially varying coefficient model (QSVCM) for the regression analysis of spatial data. The proposed model enables researchers to assess the dependence of conditional quantiles of the response variable on covariates while accounting for spatial nonstationarity. Our approach facilitates learning and interpreting heterogeneity in spatial data distributed over complex or irregular domains. We introduce a quantile regression method that utilizes bivariate penalized splines in triangulation to estimate unknown functional coefficients. We establish the L 2 convergence of the proposed estimators, demonstrating their optimal convergence rate under certain regularity conditions. An efficient optimization algorithm is developed using the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). We develop wild residual bootstrap-based pointwise confidence intervals for the QSVCM quantile coefficients. Furthermore, we construct reliable conformal prediction intervals for the response variable using the proposed QSVCM. Simulation studies show the remarkable performance of the proposed methods. Lastly, we illustrate the practical applicability of our methods by analyzing the mortality dataset and the supplementary particulate matter (PM) dataset in the United States.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Spatially varying coefficient models (SVCMs) offer a flexible extension of linear regression models to capture the non-stationarity of regression coefficients across space. Although there has been extensive research on SVCMs in estimation and hypothesis testing, most existing work has focused primarily on mean regression scenarios. In SVCMs, the relationship between the response and covariates is established through a regression, where the coefficients are allowed to vary across locations and are modeled as nonparametric functions of spatial coordinates. In the context of spatial mean regression, Gelfand et al. (2003) developed a Bayesian procedure that models the spatially varying coefficient function as a realization of a spatial process, assuming a specific prior distribution for the coefficients. Bivariate smoothing tools have also been developed to fit SVCMs in spatial regression analysis. For instance, Fotheringham et al. (2002) proposed a geographically weighted regression (GWR), which obtains the coefficient function locally at each location by minimizing weighted least squares using distance-decay weights. Mu et al. (2018) and Yu et al. (2024) developed computationally efficient global and distributed learning methods that use bivariate spline smoothing over triangulation (BST; Lai and Wang, 2013) to effectively approximate coefficient functions and accommodate complex domains with irregular boundaries.

Mean regression models the mean response as a function of covariates, disregarding the complete distributional properties of the response. However, assuming that the effect of covariates is the same across all quantiles of the distribution lacks practical and theoretical justification. Mean regression models often provide an incomplete picture of the relationships between variables. This is especially problematic for regression analyses with heterogeneous variances, which are common in spatial data analysis. To address this limitation and gain a more comprehensive insight into the effect of covariates on the response variable, quantile regression (Koenker, 2005) provides a valuable approach. This paper develops a theory and methodology for quantile SVCMs (QSVCMs) to account for the complexity of spatial data distributed over irregular and complex domains.

Various smoothing methods have been applied to quantile regression in the literature, including univariate local polynomials in Honda (2004) and Cai and Xu (2008); smoothing splines in He et al. (1998); univariate B-splines in He and Shi (1994) and Kim (2007); penalized univariate B-splines (Psplines) in Bollaerts et al. (2006) and Andriyana et al. (2014). He and Shi (1996) proposed a bivariate tensor product B-splines for a partly linear model. However, the limitation of tensor product B-splines is that they use a rectangular grid of control points, implicitly defining the function's domain as a rectangle, which may not fully capture significant features in the data that are not aligned with the major axes. Another approach proposed by Koenker and Mizera (2004) involves penalized triograms, which employ piecewise linear bivariate splines with total variation regularization in quantile regression. However, due to the jump discontinuities of piecewise linear functions and the L 1 -nature of the total variation penalty, this approach may encounter challenges when estimating functions with many fluctuations or rapid changes.

As a natural extension of bivariate quantile regression, QSVCMs have been studied, but mainly under the Bayesian framework (Reich et al., 2011;Lum et al., 2012;Yang and He, 2015). Frequentist approaches include geographically weighted quantile regression (GWQR) (Chen et al., 2012) and the semiparametric framework to approximate spatial conditional regression using a local linear method (Lu et al., 2014). Although many conventional smoothing tools are useful in the non-/semi-parametric literature, they often suffer from the problem of "leakage" when the domain of interest is complex (Ramsay, 2002;Wood et al., 2008), which refers to poor estimation over complex regions by inappropriate linking of parts of the domain separated by physical barriers.

To address this issue, we adopt the bivariate penalized splines over triangulation (BPST) method, which has been effectively applied in various contexts (Lai and Wang, 2013;Wang et al., 2020;Yu et al., 2019;Mu et al., 2018;Kim and Wang, 2021;Kim et al., 2021). Unlike traditional methods limited to simple tensorized domains, the proposed BPST method extends the analysis to complex spatial domains through triangulation. This approach adaptively fits spatial contours and features, thus preserving essential spatial relationships and avoiding boundary effects. Such capabilities lead to more accurate estimations, particularly in environments where geographical discontinuities significantly influence underlying processes. Moreover, the use of bivariate spline basis functions also provides flexibility to choose degrees and smoothness so that the proposed estimators can achieve the optimal convergence rate under certain regularity assumptions.

To achieve the desired approximation power of functions of interest, we employ a combination of the L 1 -type of the quantile loss function and the L 2 -type of roughness penalty. Quantile regression analysis for this class of SVCMs is technically challenging as commonly used algorithms for penalized mean and quantile regression are not applicable. We overcome this computational challenge by adopting the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). In addition, a wild bootstrap procedure is proposed to construct pointwise confidence intervals (PCIs) for the spatially varying quantile coefficient functions. Furthermore, reliable conformal prediction intervals for the response variable are constructed using the proposed QSVCM.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we introduce the quantile SVCMs and the BPST estimators and establish the asymptotic properties of the proposed estimators. Section 3 describes the computational algorithm. Section 4 discusses implementation details, such as the selection of triangulation, spline basis functions, and roughness penalty parameters. In addition, it presents the construction of PCIs for quantile coefficient functions and conformal prediction intervals for the response variable. In Section 5, we perform simulation studies to evaluate the finite sample performance of the proposed methods. Section 6 applies the methods to a case study on mortality data. Section 7 presents some discussion and conclusions. Detailed proofs, application of the method to the particulate matter (PM) data, and additional numerical results can be found in the Supplementary Material.

div.head: Methodology
div.p: In this section, we introduce a QSVCM and provide a review of the bivariate spline approximation on triangulation. We then propose a penalized estimator for bivariate coefficient functions in the quantile SVCM based on the quantile objective function and the thin-plate spline penalty. Furthermore, we establish the convergence rate of the proposed penalized spline coefficient estimator.

It allows for a more comprehensive understanding of the data by capturing complex quantile-specific variations in the relationships, offering valuable insights into the spatial patterns and heterogeneity of the data distribution.

div.head: Bivariate Penalized Spline Quantile Regression
div.p: Penalized methods are known to be effective for handling sparse data regions and balancing the model fitting and roughness of the function of interest. In the context of penalized spline quantile regression, we describe the estimation of bivariate quantile varying coefficients β 0, τ ⋅ , …, β p, τ ⋅ . For univariate smoothing in the mean regression, the integral of the squared curvature of the function is usually considered a penalty to balance between the model fitting and roughness of a function. In the quantile regression literature, to tackle computational challenges with the squared curvature penalty, Koenker et al. (1994) proposed using the total variation penalty based on the integral of the absolute value of the curvature and solved it as a linear program.

For bivariate smoothing, a commonly considered L 2 type penalty function for surface smoothing is the thin-plate spline penalty (Green and Silverman, 1993), also known as the energy functional, which is an extension of the classical integral of squared curvature of a univariate smooth function. Specifically, it outlines strategies for selecting tuning parameters and triangulation and describes methods employed to construct pointwise confidence intervals (PCIs) for the coefficient functions and conformal prediction intervals for the response variables.

Then, we refine the selection of λ k * considering another 10-point grid around it, with the values of log 10 λ k equally spaced between log 10 10 -2 λ k * and log 10 10 2 λ k * . The final roughness parameter vector that minimizes the k-fold CV of GACV is then chosen. To reduce computational burden, the same values of λ k and λ k * are jointly selected for each k in this study.

Triangulation selection is crucial for balancing between estimation accuracy and computational efficiency. The maxmin-angle criterion, as suggested by Lai and Schumaker (2007), can be used to maximize the minimum angle in the triangulation. In the theoretical framework, we consider Assumption (A5), which relates to π-quasi-uniform triangulation in terms of ensuring similar shapes and sizes of triangles in the triangulation. This characterization helps identify an optimal triangulation. In practice, we adopt the Delaunay triangulation algorithm to find a well-balanced triangulation mesh regarding the number, size, and shape of triangles occurring in the triangulation. Delaunay triangulations can be generated using various packages, such as the MATLAB program distmesh2d.m, delaunay.m or the MATHEMATICA function DelaunayTriangulation. For our implementation, we use the MATLAB program distmesh2d.m for Delaunay triangulation.

Our numerical studies suggest that a minimum number of triangles is necessary to adequately capture the signal from the function. However, once this minimum threshold is reached, further refinement of the triangulation typically has a negligible effect on fitting for large sample sizes. For practical applications with higher-degree BPST smoothing, we suggest setting the number of triangles as N n = min cn 2/ 2d + 4 , n/10 , where c is a tuning parameter. We find that c ∈ 3, 20 works well if the boundary is not overly complex, and c > 20 is suitable for complex domains, such as the horseshoe domain in Simulation Example 2. Using the recommended values of N n , multiple Delaunay triangulation options spanning various fineness levels can be generated. In practice, one can also start with a coarse triangulation and gradually increase the triangulation fineness to see how the k-fold CV errors or GACV values in (11) change. The final triangulation can be selected as the one that yields satisfactory predictive performance while staying within the available computing resources. It is essential to strike a balance between accuracy and computational efficiency to ensure that the analysis can be conducted effectively and efficiently.

The choice of parameters d and r also plays a crucial role in interpreting the estimated functions. When the objective is to visualize the signal-to-noise ratio or suggest a simple parametric model with constant coefficients or a semiparametric model with both constant and varying coefficients, a slightly oversmoothed function may be more suitable. In this case, the user may subjectively choose the smoothness parameter and degree of the spline function. On the other hand, when the aim is to accurately estimate the coefficient functions and preserve local structures, using a higher-order spline can be beneficial. This approach allows the model to capture more complex patterns in the data, improving the accuracy of the estimate while preserving important local details. In particular, when the underlying function is believed to be smooth, a higher-order spline with r = 1 and a degree of d ≥ 3 is recommended. The bivariate spline estimator with d = 5 has been shown to achieve the full estimation power asymptotically according to Lai and Schumaker (2007). By balancing smoothness and flexibility, we ensure that the estimator remains smooth while capturing essential local features in the data.

In summary, the selection of the tuning parameters and triangulation is important for our proposed estimation method. In the implementation, our procedure begins by selecting an appropriate spectrum of triangulations ranging from coarse to fine, tailored to the unique spatial characteristics of the data. For each triangulation setting, we independently optimize the smoothness and penalty tuning parameters and calculate the k-fold CV or GACV for each possible configuration. The configuration that yields the lowest score is designated as the optimal setup.

div.head: Pointwise Confidence Intervals (PCIs)
div.p: PCIs provide useful information about unknown coefficient functions compared to a single estimated surface. However, obtaining asymptotic distributions for the BPST estimators and constructing PCIs for the coefficient functions is challenging, and existing work is rather limited. While Lai and Wang (2013) has derived the asymptotic distributions for the unpenalized bivariate spline estimators and the asymptotic variance for piecewise constant spline estimators, obtaining the exact standard error for general BPST estimators remains a difficult task. To address this challenge, we propose employing a wild residual bootstrap method to construct PCIs for β k, τ ⋅ 's. Our approach draws inspiration from Feng et al. (2011) on unpenalized quantile regression, and Wang et al. (2018) and Lamarche and Parker (2023) on penalized quantile regression. These studies have validated the effectiveness of the wild bootstrap method in capturing the variability and distributional characteristics of estimators within parametric frameworks.

As noted in Härdle and Bowman (1988), a primary challenge in applying wild bootstrap methods to nonparametric regression stems from bias induced by smoothing. Like other smoothing methods, the BPST smoothing also inherently introduces bias when estimating bootstrap residuals. To address this issue, we implement two strategies to mitigate bias in the bootstrap residuals: (1) employing bias correction using the Bahadur representation as suggested by Feng et al. (2011), and (2) minimizing the bias magnitude through the use of a higher degree of Bernstein polynomials and finer triangulation to obtain a more accurate initial estimate of the coefficient functions. The second approach is inspired by the resampling subject bootstrap method for univariate spline approximations discussed in Huang et al. (2002). The idea is to ensure that the bias term becomes negligible compared to its variance. Our simulation studies further corroborate the robustness and reliability of wild bootstrap-based PCIs when applied to the QSVCM.
The procedure for deriving these PCIs using the wild bootstrap method is detailed as follows:

Step 1. Based on the data Y i , X i , S i i = 1 n , fit the QSVCM and obtain the initial estimators of the coefficient functions β ˆk,τ ⋅ ; d, Δ , k = 0, …, p, using pilot degree of Bernstein polynomials d and triangulation Δ. Calculate the bootstrap residuals In Step 2, a finite-sample correction factor is applied using the Bahadur representation of the estimator. The residual ϵ ˆi τ in the wild bootstrap procedure is replaced by
div.formula: ϵ ˆi τ = Y i -X i ⊤ β τ S i ; d, Δ , i = 1, …, n. Step 2. Generate Y i * = X i ⊤ β τ S i + ξ i ϵ ˆi τ , i = 1, …, n,
ϵ ˆi τ + f ˆ0 -1 Z i ⊤ Z ⊤ Z + λI -1 Z i ψ τ ϵ ˆi τ
div.p: , where I is the identity matrix, f ⋅ is the probability density of the error variable ϵ i τ , ψ τ u = τ -I u < 0 is the score function and f ˆ0 is estimated based on the residuals using a univariate adaptive kernel density estimation method. This correction, while motivated by the assumption of i.i.d. errors, has been shown to be useful in general error models, as discussed in Feng et al. (2011).

Supplementary Section S.3.4 assesses the sensitivity of the bootstrap PCIs to variations in smoothing parameters. The simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves reliable coverage rates when: (1) polynomial degrees d and d* are sufficiently high, and (2) the triangulation is appropriately refined. Consistent with our earlier recommendations in Section 4.1, we propose implementing polynomial degrees d, d* ≥ 3 to optimize statistical performance.

div.head: Conformalized Quantile Regression (CQR)
div.p: In this section, we focus on spatial prediction of the target variable using specific locations and their associated covariates. In addition, we assess the uncertainty of these predictions by constructing prediction intervals.

Conformal prediction is a robust method for creating prediction intervals that provide valid coverage for finite samples without assuming a specific distribution. However, it tends to be overly conservative. In contrast, for heteroscedastic data, quantile regression allows the construction of prediction intervals by estimating the conditional quantile function at the quantile levels α/2 and 1 -α/2. Nevertheless, the reliability of these intervals is only ensured for particular models under certain regularity and asymptotic conditions. To gain benefits from both methods, Romano et al. (2019) proposed conformalized quantile regression (CQR), a novel approach fully adaptive to heteroscedasticity, combining conformal prediction with quantile regression, to construct prediction intervals for a response Y , with the theoretical guarantee of valid coverage. We combine conformal prediction with QSVCM and propose the following CQR algorithm for prediction.
Step 1. Randomly and non-overlappingly split a whole data index ℐ = 1,2, …, n into a training set ℐ 1 and a calibration set ℐ 2 .
Step 2. For 0 < α < 1, apply BPST to fit QSVCM and obtain the estimated α/2 and 1 -α/2 conditional quantile functions,
div.formula: Q ˆα/2 Y i | X i , S i and Q ˆ1 -α/2 Y i | X i , S i , based on Y i , X i , S i , i ∈ ℐ 1 .
div.p: Step 3. Compute the conformity scores
div.formula: E i = max Q ˆα/2 Y i | X i , S i -Y i , Y i -Q ˆ1 -α/2 Y i | X i , S i for each i ∈ ℐ 2 and obtain the Q 1 -α * E*, ℐ 2 = 1 -α 1 + 1/ ℐ 2 -th empirical quantile of E* = E i : i ∈ ℐ 2 . Step 4. Given new data X new , S new , construct the prediction interval for Y new as Q ˆα/2 Y | X new , S new -Q 1 -α * E*, ℐ 2 , Q ˆ1 -α/2 Y | X new , S new + Q 1 -α * E*, ℐ 2 .

div.head: Simulation Example 1
div.p: We compare the proposed BPST estimator for QSVCM, referred to as QBPST, with two competitors: the tensor product splines (TPS) method in He and Shi (1996) and the penalized triograms with total variation regularization (TVTRI) method in Koenker and Mizera (2004).

The TVTRI is tailored for nonparametric regression with a single bivariate function, and the TPS is constrained to lattice points distributed on rectangular domains. To ensure fair comparisons, we focus on a nonparametric regression with a single bivariate function on a square domain Ω = 0,1 × 0,1 . We generate N s = 100 × 100 equally spaced grid points and randomly select n = 1600 and n = 3600 points by selecting 40 and 60 points from each axis, respectively. We simulate the response variable from the following model: Y i = β S i + ϵ i , i = 1, …, n. Supplementary Figure S.1 (g) shows a typical example of the sampled locations S i 's. To investigate the performance for different settings, we consider two regression functions with the following forms: M1: β s = 20 1 -1 -2s 1 2 1 -1 -2s 2 2 , s ∈ Ω; M2: β s = -10sin 7π s 1 + 0.15 + 10sin 7πs 2 , s ∈ Ω .

Random errors ε i are generated from two distributions: a t distribution with two degrees of freedom, t 2 , and a mixture of normal (MN) distributions ∑ ℓ = 1 3 ω ℓ N μ ℓ , σ ℓ 2 , where ω ℓ are weights, and N μ ℓ , σ ℓ 2 are normal distributions with mean μ ℓ and variance σ ℓ 2 . The parameters are set as ω 1 , ω 2 , ω 3 = 0.1,0.8,0.1 , μ 1 , μ 2 , μ 3 = -5,0, 5 , and σ 1 2 , σ 2 2 , σ 3 2 = 4,1/2,4 .

The τ th quantile regression function is defined as β τ s = β s + F ϵ -1 τ , where F ε ⋅ denotes the distribution function of ε. We consider quantile levels τ = 0.50 and 0.75, with the true coefficient functions illustrated in Supplementary Figure S.4. For each simulation scenario, we conduct 100 Monte Carlo replications.

For the QBPST method, we employ the ADMM algorithm described in Section 3. The roughness penalty parameter λ is selected by minimizing the GACV, instead of k-fold CV, due to GACV's computational efficiency, which is crucial since estimations are replicated 100 times for each scenario. In scenario M1, we set the degree of polynomial to d = 3 and the smoothness parameter to r = 1, while in scenario M2, we increase them to d = 4 and r = 1 to account for the increased complexity of the underlying function. For each iteration of the Monte Carlo simulation, the best triangulation is selected to achieve a better approximation by choosing the triangulation with the lowest GACV value among the six triangulation candidates illustrated in Supplementary Figure S.1 (a)-(f). For the TPS method, we consider cubic B-splines with equally spaced interior knots, and the number of knots for each Monte Carlo iteration is determined by the SIC proposed by Noh et al. (2012). For the TVTRI method, the selection of the penalty parameter λ is based on the SIC proposed by Koenker and Mizera (2004). The TPS and TVTRI methods are implemented using the splines and quantreg packages with functions bs, rq, and rqss, respectively.

To evaluate the accuracy of the estimated coefficient function, we measure its error by the root mean integrated squared error (RMISE) defined as RMISE β ˆτ = Ω β ˆτ s -β τ s 2 ds 1/2 , τ ∈ 0,1 , which is estimated using Riemann sums based on 100×100 equally spaced grid points. The RMISE results for each method and scenario are summarized in Supplementary Table S.1. In general, for all methods, the RMISE decreases as the sample size increases. For the function in scenario M1, all methods perform well as expected since the domain is regular and the function is simple in this example. This simulation setup favors the TPS method since the data are generated from a rectangular domain. For both noise distributions, the TPS method performs slightly better than the TVTRI and QBPST methods. However, for scenario M2, the QBPST method outperforms the other methods as it is an effective method for estimating complex functions such as the 7-cycle sine function through its flexible degrees and various smoothness. In particular, when the sample size is n = 1600, the TPS method performs much worse compared to the other two methods. The TPS method can result in very large RMISE in some iterations due to its unreliable estimation near data boundaries, where observations are sparse. The fixed functional form of TPS can lead to overcomplex representation, resulting in overfitting when dealing with data with many local variations, such as scenario M2.

Figure 1 illustrates the contour plots of the estimated functions of the three methods for scenario M2 with error distribution t 2 and sample size n = 1600. As depicted in Figure 1 (b) and (e), traditional methods appear to have a significant bias in regions with limited samples, particularly near the upper and right boundary of the rectangle. On the other hand, the proposed method demonstrates consistent estimation even in areas with sparse samples. For scenario M1, all methods have comparable standard deviations, as shown in Supplementary Table S.1. However, in scenario M2, the TPS method has a higher standard deviation than the QBPST and TVTRI methods.

div.p: In this simulation study, a modified horseshoe domain Ω is considered following the works of Ramsay (2002) and Wood et al. (2008), as shown in Supplementary Figure S.2 (a). The domain is located within the rectangle [-1,3.5]×[-1,1], which is evenly divided into N s = 226 × 101 grid points. The coefficient functions are evaluated only at the grid points within Ω.

In addition, a simulation study is conducted that incorporates spatially correlated errors to assess their impact on the performance of our proposed methodology. Our findings suggest that spatial correlation can be effectively absorbed by the intercept function through our smoothing method, with minimal impact on other coefficient functions. Details of this study can be found in Supplementary Section S.3.5.

div.p: In this study, we focus on two quantiles: τ ∈ 0.50,0.75 and repeat the simulation 100 times. The true varying coefficient functions for scenarios M1 and M2 are depicted in the first column of Supplementary Figure We compare the performance of the BPST estimator for the QSVCM (referred to as QBPST) with that of the mean SVCM (referred to as BPST). In addition, we compare it with the geographically weighted quantile regression (GWQR) introduced in Chen et al. (2012) and the geographically weighted regression (GWR) introduced in Fotheringham et al. (2002). The latter two methods are based on local weighting schemes for quantile and mean SVCMs, respectively.

For BPST and QBPST, employing bivariate spline approximation, we set the smoothness parameter r = 1 and explored spline degrees d ranging from 2 to 5. Due to space constraints in the main text, we report only the results for d = 3. For outcomes associated with other degrees, see Supplementary Table S.2. For the triangulation, we employ two triangulation options, Δ 1 (77 triangles, 65 vertices) and Δ 2 (183 triangles, 130 vertices), as depicted in Supplementary Figure S.2 (b) and (c). For BPST, the roughness penalty parameters λ 0 and λ 1 are chosen by minimizing the GCV method as described in Mu et al. (2018). For QBPST, λ 0 and λ 1 are selected by minimizing the k-fold CV and the GACV. We report only the QBPST results based on GACV, while complete results comparing GACV and 5-fold CV are provided in Supplementary Section S.3.3. For GWR and GWQR, a Gaussian kernel function is used for geographical weighting to specify spatial neighborhoods around a sample location. The leave-one-out CV bandwidth is considered for the GWR, while the 5-fold CV bandwidth is implemented for the GWQR due to the high computational burden. The implementation is carried out through the gwr function in the spgwr package for GWR and the rq function in the quantreg package for GWQR.

To evaluate the accuracy of the estimators, we report the RMISE of the estimated coefficient functions. Due to space constraints, we only present partial results corresponding to M2 and the error distribution t 2 in Table 1. The complete results can be found in Supplementary Table S.3. The results indicate that the performance of all estimators improves as the sample size increases. The effect of triangulation on the results for the QBPST is unnoticeable since the RMISEs are almost constant for Δ 1 and Δ 2 in most scenarios. However, for the BPST, the finer triangulations dramatically reduce the RMISEs of coefficients for the t 2 error distribution. Both the BPST and QBPST outperform the GWR and GWQR for all scenarios. Furthermore, for both error distributions and all scenarios, the QBPST estimator with τ = 0.50 performs better than the BPST estimator due to the robustness of the QSVCM against extreme values and heteroscedastic errors.

The simulation results are presented in Supplementary Figure S.5 for Scenario M1 and in Figure 2 for Scenario M2. The analysis is based on a sample size of n = 2000 and triangulation Δ 2 . The figures show a typical set of estimated intercept and slope functions for the t 2 error distribution. It is clear that the estimated surfaces of both the BPST and the QBPST are pretty similar to the true surfaces for β 0, τ ⋅ . For β 1, τ ⋅ , the QBPST demonstrates great accuracy with only a slight bias on the right side of the horseshoe domain. In contrast, the BPST struggles to match the true function, particularly on the upper and lower arms of the right side of the horseshoe domain. This discrepancy is more pronounced in Scenario M2 due to the large variation in heteroscedastic error influenced by the function ζ 1 s in this area.

Our findings demonstrate that the BPST and QBPST estimators tend to have a lower bias as the sample size increases, although there may be some biases present in certain iterations, such as a boundary effect on the left ends of the arms for low values of β 1, τ ⋅ in both the quantile and mean regression methods. However, the GWR and GWQR estimates for β 0, τ ⋅ and β 1, τ ⋅ exhibit larger biases, particularly around the boundary gap between the lower and upper arms of the horseshoe domain, which is caused by the "leakage" problem. Although the estimated surfaces for the geographically weighted methods show some resemblance to their respective counterparts, the large biases raise concerns about the accuracy and reliability of these estimates.

Next, we evaluate the proposed conformal prediction intervals of the response variables Y i based on the CQR method outlined in Section 4.3. For comparison, we also consider the non-conformal prediction intervals derived from the quantiles of the GWQR method. Table 2 reports the average 5-fold CV coverage probabilities and average lengths of the 95% prediction intervals across 100 replications from the QBPST-based CQR and the GWQR methods. For CQR, the dataset in each fold is randomly partitioned into training and calibration sets of equal size. In each replication, the grid points not selected as samples are treated as the test set. From Table 2, we observe that the QBPST-based CQR achieves a coverage probability very close to the nominal 95% level. Although the GWQR provides slightly narrower prediction intervals on average, its coverage rate is generally below the nominal level, indicating that its prediction intervals may be prone to undercoverage, potentially compromising their reliability.

Our final evaluation focuses on the finite-sample behavior of the PCIs introduced in Section 4.2. Table 3 presents the average coverage rates of the 95% PCIs of β k, τ ⋅ , k = 0,1, over the domain Ω. Although the coverage of β 0,0.75 ⋅ is slightly below the nominal level of MN noise, the proposed bootstrap PCIs generally perform well, meeting the desired coverage. Supplementary Figures S.6 and S.7 depict the lower and upper bounds of the 95% PCIs for the bivariate functions in Scenarios M1 and M2, respectively. The true functions seem to lie within these bounds, providing confidence in the accuracy of the PCIs.

div.head: Application
div.p: In this section, we employ the proposed method to analyze age-adjusted mortality data for the United States. An additional application to the Particulate Matter (PM) data study is presented in the Supplementary Material due to space constraints.

The mortality dataset, as described in detail by Wang and Wang (2019), comprises demographic and socioeconomic information from a total of 3,104 counties in 48 states and the District of Columbia. Our main objective is to explore the structural heterogeneity of the mortality distribution across the United States and its relationship with related variables. We exclude Alaska and Hawaii due to their geographical remoteness from the other regions.

In this analysis, we evaluate the mortality distribution using four types of covariates based on the finding of Wang and Wang (2019): social affluence factors (Affluence), disadvantage factors (Disadvantage), violent crime rate per 1,000 population (Violent Crime), as well as the urban rate (Urban).

The response variable in the analysis is the average age-standardized mortality rate per 100 population in the period 1998-2002 (Mortality) (Mortality). To ensure numerical stability, covariates, X i , are first transformed by taking the logarithm with a small positive offset δ and then standardized. We fit the proposed quantile spatially varying model as follows:
div.formula: Q τ Mortality i | Affluence i , Disadvantage i , Violent Crime i , Urban i , S i = β 0, τ S i + β 1, τ S i Affluence i + β 2, τ S i Disadvantage i + β 3, τ S i Violent Crime i + β 4, τ S i Urban i(12)
div.p: for i = 1, …, 3104, where Q τ ⋅ | X, S is the conditional quantile function given all the covariates and spatial information and β k, τ s 's are unknown quantile bivariate functions, for k = 0, …, 4.

We use QBPST to fit the quantile regression model ( 12). For the bivariate spline basis functions, we set the degree to d = 4 and the smoothness to r = 1. For comparison, we also fit the GWQR as an alternative method, utilizing the Gaussian kernel as the weighting function.

To ensure a fair evaluation of predictive performance, we optimize the triangulation roughness and penalty parameters for the QBPST and the bandwidth for the GWQR by minimizing the 5-fold CV quantile loss function. The selected triangulation configuration comprises 459 triangles and 283 vertices, as Supplementary Figure S.3 illustrates.

Figure 3 displays the estimated maps of the coefficient functions for median regression (τ = 0.5), along with their corresponding lower and upper bounds of 95% PCIs. The Supplementary Material contains additional findings, including estimated maps and 95% PCIs for the coefficient functions at the 0.25 and 0.75 quantile levels. The spatial variation of the coefficient functions is evident from these maps. In particular, the Southeast region of the United States shows higher mortality rates for the intercept, as observed in both the QBPST and GWQR methods. These higher mortality rates can be attributed to the prevalence of specific diseases. For instance, the National Heart Lung and Blood Institute has designated several states, including Alabama, Georgia, South Carolina, and Tennessee, as the "Stroke Belt" because of their higher stroke mortality rates compared to other regions (Rich et al., 2007). In addition, some previous research has found that the states of the Southeast, including Alabama, Georgia, South Carolina, and Tennessee, are associated with higher mortality rates due to congestive heart failure and prevalence of hypertension than other states; see Obisesan et al. (2000).

The analysis reveals a positive effect of "Affluence" on the conditional median of mortality in certain regions, such as the border between California and Arizona, northeast Montana, and parts of Wisconsin and Minnesota, according to the QBPST and GWQR methods. However, the latter method estimates a more significant effect in Arizona and Montana.

The results of the analysis also indicate that in most regions, "Disadvantage" is positively correlated with the conditional median of mortality. This correlation is positively strong in North Dakota, South Dakota, and eastern Montana, while negative in the west of Texas.

Furthermore, the analysis shows that the conditional median of mortality increases with "Violent Crime" in most areas. This phenomenon has legitimacy in several aspects; for example, engaging in violent acts and being victimized are associated with higher mortality rates (Stenbacka et al., 2012), and violent crime could potentially serve as a significant social factor influencing cardiovascular health (Eberly et al., 2022). Florida and Wyoming, in particular, commonly exhibit a higher impact of "Violent Crime" on the conditional median of mortality compared to other regions, while the GWQR method shows higher effects than the QBPST method on the border between Arizona and California, Maine, Florida, and Washington. Furthermore, the QBPST results indicate that the impact of "Urban" on the conditional median of mortality is substantial in Arizona and New Mexico. Especially some states in New England, such as New York and Pennsylvania, show a significantly negative impact of "Urban" on the median mortality. In particular, in the boundaries between Arizona and California, the impacts of "Urban" and "Violent Crime" on the conditional median of mortality are significantly different for the QBPST and GWQR methods. More specifically, in this region, estimates based on the GWQR method exhibit abrupt and drastic changes, whereas those from the QBPST method demonstrate smoother and more gradual changes. These gradual changes observed with QBPST, supported by enhanced in-sample accuracy and 5-fold CV metrics (see Supplementary Table S.9), better reflect the gradual impact expected from urbanization and crime rates on mortality rates. Supplementary Table S.9 presents the in-sample and 5-fold CV accuracy measures for the QBPST and GWQR methods. The standard errors for the in-sample prediction error range from 0.0135% to 0.0352%, while those for 5-fold CV prediction errors range from 0.0172% to 0.0422%. The results show that the proposed QBPST outperforms the GWQR in terms of prediction accuracy across different measures and quantile levels. One possible reason behind this phenomenon could be the impact of boundary effects in estimating the GWQR.

In Figure 3, the estimated coefficient functions of the GWQR are less effectively smoothed at certain boundaries, for example, Affluence, Disadvantage, and Violent Crime in Maine, and the boundaries between Arizona and California for Affluence, Violent Crime and Urban, Florida for Violent Crime and Urban.

Supplementary Table S.10 reports the average 5-fold CV coverage probabilities and lengths of the 95% prediction intervals constructed using the QBPST-based CQR and the GWQR methods. For CQR, in each fold, the dataset is equally partitioned into training and calibration sets. Consistent with the simulation studies, we observe that the QBPST-based CQR achieves coverage probabilities near the nominal level. In contrast, while GWQR often produces slightly narrower prediction intervals, its coverage rates generally fall below the nominal level.

div.head: Conclusions and Discussion
div.p: This paper proposes a new method for estimating and making inferences on QSVCMs. The BPST smoothing technique was employed to approximate the unknown coefficient functions. Under certain regularity conditions, our estimator showed an optimal convergence rate in terms of L 2 convergence. Our approach shows superior finite sample properties compared to alternative methods and effectively addresses the issue of leakage over complex domains. In addition, we develop PCIs for our estimators using a wild residual-based bootstrap approach. Moreover, utilizing the QSVCM-based CQR approach, we successfully construct conformal prediction intervals for the response variable that attain coverage rates nearly identical to the nominal level. Overall, our method offers a novel and robust approach to estimate and make inferences about QSVCMs.

Despite these advancements, our model assumes the independence of errors across locations once the regression function, accounting for spatial variations, is extracted. While this assumption streamlines the modeling process, it might not fully capture the complexities of real-world data, where residual spatial correlations could persist and affect both the accuracy and validity of the model. To address this, we can consider integrating a spatial autoregressive varying coefficient model, as in Mu et al. (2020) and Yu et al. (2022). However, this integration poses significant challenges, requiring complex methodological extensions and careful theoretical and computational development. Therefore, we plan to tackle this enhancement in future work.

Future work will address the theoretical foundation for applying the wild bootstrap method to construct PCIs for QSVCM coefficient functions. Research by Feng et al. (2011), Wang et al. (2018), and Lamarche and Parker (2023) has validated the effectiveness of this method in capturing estimator variability and distributional characteristics, particularly in settings with adaptive L 1 penalties. However, these theoretical results are primarily for parametric or linear regression settings and do not directly extend to our nonparametric framework. A primary challenge in applying wild bootstrap methods to nonparametric regression emerges from the bias inherent in the BPST smoothing, particularly the difficulty in deriving an asymptotic bias expression-a challenge not encountered in kernel smoothing methods (Härdle and Bowman, 1988). This problem remains unresolved even in pure approximation theory when smoothing a single bivariate function based on noise-free data. While our extensive simulations have consistently demonstrated the robust and reliable performance of our approach in practical applications, developing robust theoretical foundations for the wild bootstrap method in nonparametric quantile regression remains a critical need and requires extensive and focused research, which may merit a separate publication.

Another exciting avenue for future research involves extending our proposed QSVCMs to a spatiotemporal setting, where both spatial and temporal variations of coefficients are considered. This can be achieved by incorporating time-varying covariates and/or temporal trends into the model. The main challenge in this extension will be to deal with the high dimensionality of the spatiotemporal data and to ensure the computational feasibility of the model. It will also be interesting to study the performance of the proposed quantile estimator in the spatiotemporal context and to explore the potential of the bivariate spline approximation in this setting. Further investigations into the theoretical properties of the estimators and the development of appropriate inference methods for the spatiotemporal case will also be important for establishing the credibility of the proposed approach in this context.
